lessons.title: Close-up: a sword and a standard

zoom.label: A grey-bearded rider among the horses on the right

c1.text: Level one: the battle stops. Now zoom in on the right, among the horses: an old rider has his hand on his sword.

zoom.label: A grey-bearded rider among the horses on the right

c1q.text: What is he doing with his sword?

choices.label: Putting it back in its sheath

sources.title: J. L. Jules David, Le peintre Louis David, vol. 1 (Paris, 1880), ch. VI, reprinting J.-L. David's 1799 leaflet 'Le Tableau des Sabines' (our translations)
Musée du Louvre, collection record INV 3691, 'Les Sabines' (description quoting the Luxembourg museum catalogue of 1820; our translations)
E.-J. Delécluze, Louis David, son école et son temps. Souvenirs (Paris: Didier, 1855), ch. VII (our translations)
Livy, The History of Rome, book I, ch. 13, translated by D. Spillan (London: Bohn, 1853), Project Gutenberg
Plutarch, Life of Romulus, translated by John Dryden (The Internet Classics Archive, MIT)

c1m.text: In the middle of a battle, a commander puts his sword away: the peace has begun.

c1a.text: In a battle that's the instinct, but this blade is going in.

correction.tempting: His fist is raised high on the hilt in the thick of a battle, as if pulling the blade out.
correction.truth: He is putting it away. David's leaflet calls him the general of the cavalry; the 1820 catalogue says the gesture signals the peace.
correction.evidence: David's 1799 leaflet; the 1820 catalogue quoted in the Louvre record; Delécluze (1855): 'the general of the cavalry putting his sword back in its sheath'.

c1b.text: Yes. David's leaflet calls him the general of the cavalry, putting his sword back in its sheath; the 1820 catalogue says he signals the peace.

c1c.text: The fighting is ending, but this isn't a surrender.

correction.tempting: His head is bowed and his blade is coming down, as if he were giving up.
correction.truth: He is sheathing it to signal peace. In the legend, both sides make a truce and become one people.
correction.evidence: David's leaflet and the 1820 catalogue: he puts his sword back in its sheath, signalling peace. Livy and Plutarch: a truce, then one state.

zoom.label: High above the spears on the right

c2.text: Level one: Romulus stands on the right with his Romans. Now look up, above their spears: a bundle of hay, tied to a pole.

zoom.label: High above the spears on the right

c2q.text: Why would soldiers carry a bundle of hay on a pole?

sources.title: Musée du Louvre, collection record INV 3691, 'Les Sabines' (description quoting the Luxembourg museum catalogue of 1820; our translations)
Plutarch, Life of Romulus, translated by John Dryden (The Internet Classics Archive, MIT)
Livy, The History of Rome, book I, ch. 12, translated by D. Spillan (London: Bohn, 1853), Project Gutenberg

c2m.text: David's Romans fight under one of their very first standards: a bundle of hay.

c2a.text: Horses rear just below it, but it isn't for them.

correction.tempting: Horses rear just below it, and hay is what horses eat.
correction.truth: It's a standard: the 1820 catalogue calls it one of the Romans' first standards, and Plutarch explains the custom.
correction.evidence: 1820 catalogue, quoted in the Louvre record: 'one of the first standards of this people'. Plutarch: captains carried bundles of grass on poles, called manipuli.

c2b.text: Yes. Plutarch says Romulus's captains each carried 'a small bundle of grass and shrubs tied to a pole', called manipuli. The 1820 catalogue calls it an early Roman standard.

c2c.text: Romulus does pray to Jupiter in this battle, but this isn't an offering.

correction.tempting: In the legend, Romulus prays to Jupiter during this very battle and vows him a temple.
correction.truth: The hay is a military standard: Plutarch says Romulus's captains carried bundles of grass on poles, called manipuli.
correction.evidence: Plutarch, Life of Romulus (Dryden's translation). The 1820 catalogue, quoted in the Louvre record: 'one of the first standards' of the Romans.

c1q.what_you_learn: Among the horses on the right, the general of the cavalry puts his sword back in its sheath: the gesture that signals the peace.

c1q.confidence: High: three independent texts (David's leaflet, the 1820 catalogue, Delécluze) single out this gesture, and the photo shows one rider with a blade above a scabbard.
c1q.notes: Ledger claims sabines-008 (leaflet, 1820 catalogue, Delécluze), sabines-016 (truce and union: Livy and Plutarch). Which rider he is, is our reading of the photograph (the ledger says so); no source gives left or right, but no other figure sheathes a sword. The 1820 catalogue's 'vieux commandant' and the grey beard in the crop agree. Delécluze's note that the public admired this figure is single-source and is not used on screen. The crop's label names the place only.

extends.concept: Iconography: from who is who (level) to the oldest emblem in the picture, a bundle of hay as a Roman standard

c2q.what_you_learn: The bundle of hay on a lance above the Roman ranks is one of Rome's first standards: Plutarch says Romulus's captains carried bundles of grass on poles, called manipuli.

c2q.confidence: High for the meaning (the 1820 catalogue and Plutarch agree independently); the picture's standard matches the catalogue's 'bundle of hay tied to a lance'. Plutarch places the custom in Romulus's band before Rome was founded; the screen says only that his captains carried such bundles.
c2q.notes: Ledger claims sabines-011 (1820 catalogue and Plutarch: the common core, a hay bundle on a pole as an early Roman standard), sabines-009 (our looking: the bundle over the crowd at right), sabines-010 (the catalogue places it among the Roman standards; single, used only for placement), sabines-015 (Romulus's prayer to Jupiter Stator, Livy and Plutarch). The wolf standard is cut out of the crop. The fodder and offering options are real alternatives a viewer reaches for; their cards state only sourced facts.
